title: A page for everything on /streaming/
audience: Dinis, on an iPad or iPhone
summary: The streaming page is live, and under it sit 166 titles and 888 people that link to each other. Dinis agreed a static page per entity plus one graph file; this story shows why, and asks how open the data can be under TMDB's terms.

beats.narration: The streaming page on the data site is live. It lists 281 titles from Netflix, Disney plus, Prime Video and Apple TV plus, in the UK and Portugal, read from TMDB when the site is built, for display only.

Under the page sit 320 list rows but only 166 different titles: 92 films and 74 series. There are 888 people, and 77 of them are in more than one title. That overlap is what makes a graph worth drawing.

Four ways to give everything a page. A, one file and a router. B, the 404 trick, where every page really answers 404. C, a static page per entity. D, those pages plus one small graph file. Dinis agreed D.

items: A: one file and a router in the page
C: a static page per entity
D: C plus one graph file (agreed)

beats.narration: A prototype of D, built from the live data: 1,143 pages and 3,167 links, with not one broken link. Each page is about 1.8 kilobytes and draws its own small graph. The graph file is 42 kilobytes compressed.

visual.label: pages in the prototype, 0 broken links

beats.narration: The ontology follows schema.org. People link to films and series as actor, director or creator. Titles link to genres, which roll up into seven families, and to catalogues: one service in one country.

Three fixes come first. Keep TMDB's person ids, so two people with one name stay apart. Give each title an address from its TMDB id, since its name differs by country. And merge TMDB's film and TV genres into one list.

items: Address each title by its TMDB id
One genre list for films and series

beats.narration: TMDB's terms count handing a data set of their content to others as commercial use. So the pages stay HTML, for display. The open part of the graph could come from Wikidata, which anyone may reuse, and be served as JSON.

left.title: Now: TMDB, display only
points: Graph file used by our pages only

right.title: Next: Wikidata, CC0
points: Who is in what, genres, countries
Served as JSON in our API
TMDB adds only where it streams

decision.question: How open should the streaming graph's data be?

options.label: HTML pages only
bad: No JSON for other sites or agents

options.label: HTML now, Wikidata JSON next
bad: A second source to collect and match by TMDB id
blocks: The TMDB TV series id property on Wikidata, not yet checked

options.label: JSON of TMDB content
bad: Counts as commercial under TMDB's terms as read

decision.why: It keeps TMDB to display, as Dinis chose, and still gives the graph an open JSON layer that other sites and agents can reuse.

answer.where: his voice memo, recorded by maestro.d
answer.words: the graph should always be open ... From our side, it should be JSON that we provide out ... Wikidata. Okay, I agree ... Wikidata is usually quite late ... we kind of need real-time data
answer.note: JSON out first, then HTML; Wikidata yes, but near-real-time sources are needed too. Recorded in board/team/maestro.d/decisions/2026-11-22-voice-memo-18-answers.md; data.d reads which option this is.
